composition: Quaternary Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steel with nominal composition (wt%) Al 9, Mn 10, C 0.4, Fe balance — i.e. 9Al-10Mn-0.4C. Aluminium is the principal density-reducing element (Fe–Mn–Al–C steels can cut density by more than 20 wt% when sufficiently alloyed), and it also acts as a ferrite former and promotes κ-carbide formation; Mn and C are austenite stabilizers added to improve microstructure and mechanical properties, while the Al–C combination supplies the chemical driving force for κ-carbide precipitation. This composition lies within the tested grade ranges of the study (Al 9–12 wt%, Mn 10/20/30 wt%, C 0.4–1 wt%, Fe balance) and represents the leanest-carbon end of that range.
conclusions: Within the study this hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-0.4C sample provides the as-received, 1150 °C-equilibrium reference for the Fe–Mn–Al–C grade family. Its key contribution is thermodynamic: because the austenite (FCC_A1) fraction of this composition does not decrease at 800 °C relative to 1150 °C, the grade does not undergo austenite decomposition during 800 °C tempering, whereas the drop of the austenite fraction from 1150 °C to 600 °C underlies the partial discontinuous precipitation observed in the same composition at 600 °C. The overall study concludes that triggering a given austenite decomposition requires a sufficient combination of chemical driving force (Al–C content), thermal energy input (tempering temperature) and thermodynamic stability of austenite, and that raising carbon (0.4 → 1 wt%) as well as Al and Mn content shifts the reaction type from discontinuous precipitation toward cellular transformation and spinodal decomposition; for the low-density Fe–Mn–Al–C system this enables density reductions above 20 wt% plus potential cryogenic, oxidation- and wear-resistance applications, at the cost of a complex and composition-sensitive metallurgy.
mechanisms: Hot-rolling at 1150 °C followed by water quenching fixes the as-received reference state at the 1150 °C equilibrium assemblage of BCC_A2 (δ-ferrite), FCC_A1 (austenite) and KAPPA_E21 (κ-carbide); all subsequent tempering behaviour of this composition is judged against this starting equilibrium.

Because the FCC_A1 (austenite) fraction of the 9Al-10Mn-0.4C composition does not decrease at 800 °C compared with 1150 °C in the CALPHAD phase-fraction diagram, there is no thermodynamic gradient driving austenite decomposition at 800 °C — which explains why this grade does not transform during 800 °C tempering even though the higher temperature should give faster kinetics.

The austenite (FCC_A1) fraction of this composition decreases from 1150 °C down to 600 °C, creating a thermodynamic gradient that drives the partial austenite decomposition (discontinuous precipitation into γ + κ lamellae) reported for this grade at 600 °C.

Discontinuous precipitation is a grain-boundary-migration reaction that does not change the composition of the untransformed parent austenite and produces lamellar γ + κ-carbide products nucleating at grain boundaries; the lower driving force at the lower annealing temperature (600 °C) allows grain-boundary migration of the forming lamellar phase rather than complete lamellar separation.

Chemical composition is fundamental because it not only supplies the Al–C driving force for κ-carbide precipitation but also fixes the phase equilibria among which tempering can operate; the lean 0.4 wt% C content of this grade keeps its Al–C driving force lower than that of the 1C grades, limiting the extent of austenite decomposition.

Austenite stability in Fe–Mn–Al–C steels is governed by Mn and C; since the Mn and C concentrations in this medium-Mn, low-C grade are not high enough to fully stabilize austenite against its own transformation, decomposition becomes possible once sufficient thermal energy input (tempering) and Al–C driving force are supplied.
microstructure: No micrograph of the as-hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-0.4C is reported; the structure of this reference condition was assessed thermodynamically. Per the CALPHAD phase-volume-fraction diagram for the 9Al-10Mn-0.4 composition over 0–1300 °C, the equilibrium assemblage consists of BCC_A2 (δ-ferrite), FCC_A1 (austenite) and KAPPA_E21 (κ-carbide): δ-ferrite holds ~0.87–0.92 mol below ~700 °C, passes through a minimum of ~0.51 mol at 800 °C and falls to ~0.28 mol at 1300 °C; austenite is near zero up to ~700 °C, rises steeply to ~0.49 mol at 800 °C and declines to ~0.28 mol at 1300 °C; κ-carbide amounts to ~0.10 mol between 200 and 700 °C and vanishes near 850 °C. The as-hot-rolled (as-received) state is taken to correspond to the 1150 °C equilibria. No grain-size, texture, precipitate or defect data specific to the hot-rolled condition are reported for this composition.
processing: The alloy was produced by casting in a 100 kW vacuum induction furnace, yielding 0.5 kg ingots. The ingots were then hot-rolled at 1150 °C to 5 mm flat products, followed by water quenching — this as-hot-rolled plus quenched state is the as-received (reference) condition of this sample. (Sibling samples of the same alloy were subsequently heat treated at 600 °C and 800 °C for 30 min followed by water quenching; those tempering treatments produced the decomposition microstructures, not this hot-rolled reference state.) Thin sections were prepared by through-thickness embedding, grinding and polishing, performed separately for the hot-rolled and heat-treated states.
properties: No Vickers macro-hardness value is tabulated for the 9Al-10Mn-0.4C composition in any condition (the hardness tables report values only for the 1C grades). Characterisation of the alloys across processing conditions combined optical microscopy, SEM secondary-electron imaging (SEI) with EDX/EDS for phase morphology and local chemical composition, and Vickers macro-hardness testing at a 5 kg load with 5 indentations per sample (the hardness data being treated statistically with Minitab18®), supported by CALPHAD phase-volume-fraction calculations used for thermodynamic interpretation. None of the reported property or characterisation results are attributed specifically to the hot-rolled 9Al-10Mn-0.4C state.
summary: The 9Al-10Mn-0.4C hot-rolled sample is a vacuum-cast Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steel of nominal composition Fe–9Al–10Mn–0.4C (wt%) that was hot-rolled at 1150 °C to 5 mm flat products and water quenched, giving the as-received (reference) condition. In a study devoted to austenite decomposition in Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels, this low-carbon, medium-Mn grade defines the 1150 °C equilibrium reference state against which the tempered microstructures of the alloy family are compared.
unmapped: The γ + κ lamellar microstructure reported for the 9Al-10Mn-0.4C composition (only partial discontinuous precipitation starting at the grain boundaries, Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 2(a)) was measured after 600 °C tempering and therefore belongs to the 600 °C tempered sibling sample, not to this as-hot-rolled (1150 °C) sample.
The paper explicitly states that the 9Al-10Mn-0.4C alloy did not undergo austenite decomposition during tempering at 800 °C.

No Vickers hardness value is tabulated for the 9Al-10Mn-0.4C composition in any condition; Tables 2, 4, 5, 8 and 9 report hardness only for the 9Al-10Mn-1C, 12Al-10Mn-1C, 12Al-20Mn-1C, 12Al-30Mn-1C, 9Al-20Mn-1C and 9Al-30Mn-1C grades.

The reported as-hot-rolled microstructure of this sample is inferred from the CALPHAD phase-volume-fraction diagram for 9Al-10Mn-0.4 (which the authors note is indicative and qualitative, because hot-rolled conditions at 1150 °C are not identical to the simulated equilibrium).
